title: URL Shortener
objectives: Scope URL Shortener: create short link from long url, redirect short link to original
Size it: 100M redirects/day, about 5,800/s at peak
Defend the design: generate ids with a counter/snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5t ids)

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 75 · URL Shortener: A short-link service for SMS links sent by Indian banks and shopping apps, where a 160-character SMS cannot fit a long tracking URL. In scope: Create short link from long URL; Redirect short link to original; Optional custom alias & expiry.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 75 non-functionals: Redirect p99 < 50 ms. 100:1 read/write. Links never collide. Out of scope: Link-in-bio pages and QR design; Full marketing analytics dashboards.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 75 reference path: Generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5T ids). → Store id → URL in a key-value store; cache hot links in Redis; 301/302 redirect. → Async click analytics via a queue; CDN/edge caching for viral links.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 75 risks: Id generation: Hashing the long URL and truncating causes collisions that need retries; a counter or Snowflake id encoded in base62 never collides. 301 versus 302: 301 is cached by browsers, which cuts load but hides repeat clicks from analytics and makes link edits sticky; 302 keeps every click visible.

questions.prompt: The create-link call (POST /v1/links) times out on a phone and the app retries. How do you avoid making two short links?

choices.label: Send an Idempotency-Key; the server returns the stored result on retry
Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate request
Generate the short code on the client from the current time
Raise the client timeout so the app never needs to retry

questions.explanation: The first request may have succeeded before the timeout. An idempotency key lets the server recognise the retry and return the same short link; TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart.

questions.prompt: A link goes viral and redirects jump 10× with no cache in front of the store. What saturates first?

diagramNodes.label: KV store partition for that code

questions.explanation: Every redirect for one code hits the same key, so one partition of the store takes the whole spike. Stateless redirect servers scale out; caching the hot code in Redis or at the edge absorbs it.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism guarantees two new links never get the same short code?

choices.label: Let each server count from one on its own
Pick a random code and hope collisions stay rare
Pre-allocated counter ranges per server, encoded in base62
Hash the long URL and keep the first seven characters

questions.explanation: Counter ranges handed out by a coordinator are unique by construction. Truncated hashes and random codes collide and need a check-and-retry; independent counters repeat.

questions.prompt: Marketing wants every click counted, while ops wants the fewest redirect requests. Which redirect fits marketing?

choices.label: 302, so every click reaches the service and is counted
301, so browsers cache the redirect and later clicks skip you
Client-side JavaScript redirect after the page fully loads
200 with the long URL in the body for the client to follow

questions.explanation: A 301 is cached by browsers, so repeat clicks never reach the service and are not counted. A 302 keeps every click visible at the cost of more traffic.

title: Pastebin
objectives: Scope Pastebin: create a paste, read a paste by id
Size it: 15M reads/day, about 520/s at peak
Defend the design: metadata in sql, content in object storage

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 76 · Pastebin: Share code snippets and logs between developers, with expiry, like Pastebin or a GitHub gist. In scope: Create a paste; Read a paste by ID; Expire pastes.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 76 non-functionals: Reads p99 < 100 ms. Durable storage. Read-heavy. Out of scope: Real-time collaborative editing; Code execution of pastes.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 76 reference path: Metadata in SQL, content in object storage. → Cache popular pastes; CDN for raw views. → TTL cleanup worker deletes expired pastes.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 76 risks: Content in the database or object storage?: Small pastes could live in SQL, but object storage keeps the database small, makes backups fast and lets a CDN serve public pastes directly; metadata stays in SQL for queries by owner and expiry. Unguessable ids: Sequential ids let anyone scrape private pastes; random ids from a large space (62 to the power 8 ≈ 218 trillion) make guessing impractical.

questions.prompt: Creating a paste (POST /v1/pastes) times out and the client retries. How do you avoid two copies?

choices.label: Raise the timeout so the client never retries
Deduplicate by comparing paste text across all users
Send an Idempotency-Key and return the first paste's id on retry
Make paste creation a GET so a repeat is harmless

questions.explanation: Only the client knows the two requests are the same attempt; an idempotency key carries that. Two users may legitimately paste the same text, so content matching is wrong.

questions.prompt: A popular paste is opened 10× more than usual and bodies are read straight from the object store on every view. What saturates first?

diagramNodes.label: Object storage reads for that key

questions.explanation: Every view fetches the same body. Putting the CDN in front of /raw/{id} serves it from the edge so the store and service barely notice.

questions.prompt: Why keep paste bodies in object storage rather than in the SQL row?

choices.label: SQL cannot store text longer than one kilobyte
Object storage gives transactions across many pastes
It removes the need for a paste id altogether
Bodies are large and cold; SQL stays small and fast for metadata

questions.explanation: Most pastes are read rarely and can be megabytes. Object storage is cheap, durable and CDN-friendly; SQL keeps only the small, indexed metadata.

questions.prompt: Expired pastes must disappear. Which approach balances correctness and cost?

choices.label: Delete each paste with its own timer thread on a server
Only a nightly sweeper, with reads trusting whatever exists
Check expiry on read, and let a sweeper or lifecycle rule delete later
Never delete, just hide expired pastes in the user interface

questions.explanation: Checking on read gives exact expiry for users; the sweeper or an object-store lifecycle rule reclaims space in bulk later.

title: Rate Limiter
objectives: Scope Rate Limiter: limit requests per user/ip/key, return 429 with retry hint
Size it: 400M API calls/day, about 23,000/s at peak
Defend the design: gateway calls a rate limiter backed by redis token buckets (lua for atomicity)

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 77 · Rate Limiter: Protect the OTP and login APIs of a fintech from abuse, shared across every API server. In scope: Limit requests per user/IP/key; Return 429 with retry hint; Configurable rules.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 77 non-functionals: Adds < 5 ms latency. Highly available. Shared across instances. Out of scope: Billing and quota invoicing; Bot detection with ML.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 77 reference path: Gateway calls a rate limiter backed by Redis token buckets (Lua for atomicity). → Rules stored in SQL and cached locally. → Fail-open for non-critical APIs, fail-closed for OTP.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 77 risks: Fail open or fail closed?: Failing closed during a Redis outage blocks every login; failing open lets attackers through. Choosing keys: Indian mobile carriers put many users behind shared IPs, so per-phone and per-user limits are primary and IP limits are loose, catching only obvious floods.

questions.prompt: A client gets 429 and immediately retries in a tight loop. What should the response tell it?

choices.label: A 500 error so the client treats it as a server fault
Nothing; silently drop the connection to save work
A 200 with an empty body so the client stops retrying
A Retry-After header with when the bucket refills

questions.explanation: 429 plus Retry-After tells well-behaved clients exactly when to come back, which stops retry storms. A 500 invites more retries and a 200 lies.

questions.prompt: Traffic is 10× normal and every gateway checks a single Redis shard for every request. What saturates first?

diagramNodes.label: The single Redis shard holding the counters

questions.explanation: Every request costs a Redis round trip on one shard. Shard counters by key, or keep local token buckets that sync periodically.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism lets many gateways enforce one user's limit consistently?

choices.label: A SQL row lock taken on every single request
The client counts its own requests and reports them
An atomic token-bucket update in Redis via a Lua script
Each gateway keeps its own counter and never shares it

questions.explanation: A Lua script runs the read-check-decrement atomically in Redis, so concurrent gateways cannot both spend the last token. Local-only counters let a user exceed the limit N times over.

questions.prompt: Redis, which holds the rate-limit counters, goes down. For a login endpoint under attack, what is the safer default?

choices.label: Restart every gateway until Redis comes back
Fail open for login, so legitimate users are never blocked
Fail closed for login, so attackers cannot brute-force freely
Switch all limits off globally until someone is paged

questions.explanation: For security-sensitive endpoints, failing closed (or falling back to a strict local limit) is safer; for ordinary reads, failing open keeps the product up.

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 96 · Leaderboard: Live free-to-play fantasy-contest leaderboards during IPL matches: update scores, show rank and top N. In scope: Update scores live; Show rank and top-N; Millions per contest.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 96 non-functionals: Updates within seconds. Massive spikes at match time. Accurate final ranks. Out of scope: Reward fulfilment; Team creation UI.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 96 reference path: Score events streamed; workers update Redis sorted sets per contest. → Sharded sorted sets for huge contests; top-N cached. → Final ranks computed in batch for rewards.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 96 risks: Update fan-out: One wicket changes points for every team containing that bowler, possibly millions of teams; recomputing per team in batches every few seconds is cheaper than per ball per team in real time. Accurate final ranks: Live ranks can be approximate, but final standings use a deterministic batch computation with tie-break rules, audited before rewards are announced. Real-money contests are banned in India since the Online Gaming Act, 2025, so rewards are non-cash.

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 98 · Web Crawler: A web crawler for Indian news and e-commerce sites feeding a search engine. In scope: Fetch pages from seed URLs; Extract and enqueue links; Respect robots.txt and politeness.

cards.title: Quality bar

cards.title: Reference sketch

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 98 risks: Politeness: Partitioning the frontier by host and assigning each host to one queue enforces per-host rate limits and avoids accidentally overloading small sites. cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 102 · Distributed Message Queue: A Kafka-like distributed message log: produce, consume with offsets, retain for days. In scope: Produce messages; Consume with offsets; Retention.

cards.title: Quality bar

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 102 reference path: Partitioned append-only segments on disk, replicated with leader/followers. → Metadata/leadership via Raft. → Consumer groups track offsets.

cards.title: Failure modes

title: Distributed Counter
objectives: Scope Distributed Counter: increment a counter (likes, views), read the current count
Size it: 2B increments/day, about 120,000/s at peak
Defend the design: hot counters sharded into n sub-counters summed on read

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 114 · Distributed Counter: A distributed counter for likes and views that handles very hot counters. In scope: Increment a counter (likes, views); Read the current count; Handle very hot counters.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 114 non-functionals: Increments under 10 ms. Counts may lag by a few seconds. No lost increments. Out of scope: Per-user like history UI; Fraud detection.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 114 reference path: Hot counters sharded into N sub-counters summed on read. → Increments batched by workers before hitting storage. → Consumers idempotent per event ID.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 114 risks: No lost increments: Redis alone can lose recent writes on failover; the Kafka log or periodic durable snapshots allow counts to be rebuilt exactly. Lag versus cost: Summing 32 keys on every read is cheap with a short cache; allowing counts to lag a few seconds is what makes the design scale.
